In [[statistical process control|statistical quality control]], the '''CUSUM''' (or '''cumulative sum control chart''') is a [[sequential analysis]] technique developed by [[Ewan Stafford Page|E. S. Page]] of the [[University of Cambridge]]. It is typically used for monitoring [[change detection]].<ref name=grigg>{{cite journal
|title=The Use of Risk-Adjusted CUSUM and RSPRT Charts for Monitoring in Medical Contexts
|author=Grigg
|journal=Statistical Methods in Medical Research
|volume=12
|pages=147–170
|year=2003
|doi=10.1177/096228020301200205
|pmid=12665208
|last2=Farewell
|first2=VT
|last3=Spiegelhalter
|first3=DJ
|issue=2
|display-authors=etal}}</ref>
CUSUM was announced in [[Biometrika]], in 1954, a few years after the publication of [[Abraham Wald|Wald]]'s [[sequential probability ratio test]] (SPRT).<ref name=page>{{cite journal
|first=E. S.
|last=Page
|title=Continuous Inspection Scheme
|journal=Biometrika
|volume=41
|issue=1/2
|date=June 1954
|pages=100–115
|jstor=2333009
|doi=10.1093/biomet/41.1-2.100|hdl=10338.dmlcz/135207
|hdl-access=free
}}</ref>

Page referred to a "quality number" <math>\theta</math>, by which he meant a parameter of the [[probability distribution]]; for example, the [[mean]]. He devised CUSUM as a method to determine changes in it, and proposed a criterion for deciding when to take corrective action. When the CUSUM method is applied to changes in mean, it can be used for [[step detection]] of a [[time series]].

A few years later, [[George Alfred Barnard]] developed a visualization method, the V-mask chart, to detect both increases and decreases in <math>\theta</math>.<ref>{{cite journal
|first=G.A.
|last=Barnard
|authorlink=George Alfred Barnard
|title=Control charts and stochastic processes
|journal=[[Journal of the Royal Statistical Society]]
|volume=B (Methodological)
|issue=21, number 2
|year=1959
|pages=239–71
|doi=10.1111/j.2517-6161.1959.tb00336.x
|jstor=2983801
}}</ref>

==Method==
As its name implies, CUSUM involves the calculation of a cumulative sum (which is what makes it "sequential"). Samples from a process <math>x_n</math> are assigned weights <math>\omega_n</math>, and summed as follows:

:<math>S_0=0</math>
:<math>S_{n+1}=\max(0, S_n+x_{n+1}-\omega_n)</math>

When the value of ''S'' exceeds a certain threshold value, a change in value has been found. The above formula only detects changes in the positive direction. When negative changes need to be found as well, the min operation should be used instead of the max operation, and this time a change has been found when the value of ''S'' is ''below'' the (negative) value of the threshold value.

Page did not explicitly say that <math>\omega</math> represents the [[likelihood function]], but this is common usage.

This differs from SPRT by always using zero function as the lower "holding barrier" rather than an actual lower "holding barrier".<ref name=grigg/> Also, CUSUM does not require the use of the likelihood function.

As a means of assessing CUSUM's performance, Page defined the ''average run length'' (A.R.L.) [[figure of merit|metric]]; "the expected number of articles sampled before action is taken." He further wrote:<ref name=page/>

<blockquote>
When  the  quality  of  the output  is  satisfactory  the A.R.L.  is  a measure  of  the expense incurred by the scheme when it gives false alarms, i.e., [[Type I error]]s ([[Neyman–Pearson lemma|Neyman & Pearson]], 1936<ref>{{cite journal
|title=Sufficient statistics and uniformly most powerful tests of statistical hypotheses
|journal=[[Statistical Research Memoirs]]
|volume=I
|pages=113–137
}}</ref>).  On  the other  hand,  for  constant  poor  quality  the A.R.L.  measures  the delay and thus  the amount of scrap produced before the rectifying action is taken,  i.e., [[Type II error]]s.
</blockquote>

==Example==
The following example shows 20 observations <math>X</math> of a process with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 0.5.

From the <math>Z</math> column, it can be seen that <math>X</math> never deviates by 3 standard deviations (<math>3 \sigma</math>), so simply alerting on a high deviation will not detect a failure, whereas CUSUM shows that the <math>S_H</math> value exceeds 4 at the 17th observation.

{|
|-
! Column !! Description
|-
| <math>X</math> || The observations of the process with an expected mean <math>\bar{x}</math> of 0 and an expected standard deviation <math>\sigma_X</math> of 0.5
|-
| <math>Z</math> || The normalized observations, ''i.e.'' centered around the mean and scaled by the standard deviation <math>Z_n = \frac{X_n - \bar{x}}{\sigma_X}</math>
|-
| <math>S_H</math> || The ''high'' CUSUM value, detecting a positive anomaly, <math>{S_H}_{n+1} = \max(0, {S_H}_n + Z_{n+1} - \omega)</math> 
|-
| <math>S_L</math> || The ''low'' CUSUM value, detecting a negative anomaly, <math>{S_L}_{n+1} = \max(0, {S_L}_n - Z_{n+1} - \omega)</math>
|}

where <math>\omega</math> is a critical level parameter (tunable, same as threshold T) that's used to adjust the sensitivity of change detection: larger <math>\omega</math> makes CUSUM less sensitive to the change and vice versa.
